item.title: US solar robotics company pushes on with Australian manufacturing plans
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Luminous Robotics expects the first of at least 100 Australian-made autonomous solar panel installation robots will roll out of its new $39.7 million manufacturing facility in Melbourne by mid-2026.
item.content:encoded:
United States-based robotics company Luminous Robotics is progressing plans to establish production facilities in Melbourne where it will manufacture a fleet of robots designed to accelerate utility-scale solar deployment and reduce construction costs.

Luminous has developed a specialised robotics fleet that includes two complementary platforms designed to automate solar panel installation on large-scale solar farms. The company’s architecture includes the Pallet Lumi v2, a robotic platform that transports solar panels along the installation row, and the Install Lumi that collects the panels individually and places them onto the mounting structure.

The company said its current generation of automated robot allows for solar panels to be installed with a cycle time as low as 40 seconds.

Luminous Australia General Manager Tenzin Crouch said the application of coordinated robotics system has already been successfully trialled at large-scale solar builds in Victoria and New South Wales (NSW) and the company is now looking to scale up manufacturing.

“We have proven that these robots do work in Australia, doing some of the hardest work on site,” he said. “The next step is to turn that into scale.”

Luminous is planning to establish a $39.7 million manufacturing facility, backed by $17.8 million from Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), in Melbourne with Crouch confirming he expects to sign the lease for a factory site in the coming weeks. Fit-out will begin in early 2027, with production starting in the second quarter.

“We’ll establish that facility Q1 next year and have first robots off the production line Q2 next year,” he said, adding that the project is expected to deliver about 100 pallet and install Lumi robots by 2029.

“We have an initial production run of five robots by mid-year next year,” he said. “And then from there, that facility is targeted to produce about 15 robots every six months across both generations of the pallet and the plate installation.”

Crouch said the Lumi platform takes on the heavy, repetitive work of lifting and placing solar panels with the current generation of robots up to 2.5 times faster than existing labour practices. The company is working towards about a four times efficiency, unlocking the potential to significantly lower solar farm construction costs.

“And because the machines are electric, that would allow for overnight operations which would be a game-changer,” Crouch said, adding the shift towards commercial-scale local manufacturing is the opportunity to take robots already working alongside Australian solar crews and build them at a scale that matches the work ahead.

“There’s approximately 160 GW of projects in Australia’s development pipeline,” he said. “Even if 50% of them don’t get through DA, there’s still 80 GW over the next 10 years so there’s a lot to do.”

In addition to the Australian market, Luminous sees the Melbourne facility as a potential base to serve New Zealand, South America and Southeast Asia.

“We see Australia as a sort of export hub for the region,” Crouch said. “New Zealand is not a huge market but it’s quite growing quite a lot, Chile as well, and then obviously up into Southeast Asia.”

Luminous said the Lumi robots will be assembled and tested at the Melbourne facility, with Australian suppliers fabricating metal parts from the outset. As the fleet grows, the company will look to bring more local suppliers into production.

“It is going to start mostly as assembly, but our intent is to over the course of the project onshore a lot of the fabrication aspects of that as well,” Crouch said. “So the local supply chain is going to level up.”

item.title: Acen unveils big solar, wind, battery project for Queensland coal country
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Acen Australia is seeking federal government approval to build a renewable energy hub in central Queensland comprising a 500 MW solar facility, 440 MW of wind generation, and a 1,600 MWh battery energy storage system.
item.content:encoded:
Acen Australia, the local arm of Philippines-headquartered renewables developer Acen, has lodged documents with the federal government’s Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water seeking the tick of approval for the Belyando Energy Project planned for central Queensland.

The proposed Belyando project, being developed across an almost 1,670-hectare site about 25 kilometres southwest of the coal-mining town of Moranbah, would comprise up to 500 MW of solar generation, and a 440 MW wind farm. The project also includes a battery energy storage system (BESS) with the initial concept design sizing it at 500 MW / 1,600 MWh.

Acen said the project is “strategically located” in Queensland’s industrial heartland, is close to the existing transmission network, and is being designed to “contribute to long-term energy reliability for Queensland’s industrial backbone.” 

Acen, the owner of two of Australia’s biggest solar farms, is now seeking approval for the project through the federal Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation (EPBC) Act, which aims to protect nationally threatened species and ecological communities.

According to the impact summary for EPBC referral application, the project area is currently being used for agricultural purposes, primarily cattle grazing, and it is expected that agricultural activities will continue once the project commences operations.

Acen’s Australian portfolio already exceeds more than 1 GW capacity of large-scale renewable energy generation under construction and in operation.

The company owns the recently completed 400 MW Stubbo Solar Farm in New South Wales, and the New England Solar Farm, which is currently being increased in size from 400 MW to 720 MW. It is also constructing the 200 MW / 400 MWh New England BESS, next to the stage 1 and stage 2 solar farms, which it expects to complete in the first half of 2027.

Acen said it also has more than 13 GW of solar, wind, battery, and pumped hydro projects in the development pipeline.

item.title: Project delivery is real test of renewable energy transition
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australia is not short of renewable energy ambition. The development pipeline is substantial and delivery is accelerating. But given the capacity and escalation pressures identified in WT's latest Australian Construction Market Conditions Report – November 2026, the energy sector's challenge is increasingly one of converting investment into operating capacity.
item.content:encoded:
There has been real progress. During FY26, the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) reported the National Electricity Market (NEM) connection pipeline grew from 53 GW to 75.4 GW, and a record 9.1 GW of new generation and storage capacity reached full output. Yet the size of the pipeline alone is becoming a less useful measure of how quickly the transition is moving. What matters increasingly is how efficiently projects move from investment through delivery, connection and commissioning.

Evidence shows a strong investment case does not guarantee a deliverable project. Grid connection, network readiness, specialist capability and long-lead electrical equipment can all sit on the critical path. If those dependencies are not understood early, the commercial-operation date can quickly come under pressure.

Construction completion is not the end of the program

One issue being underestimated is the gap between finishing construction and having an asset commercially operational. A project can be substantially complete while network works, registration, testing and commissioning are still underway. Those activities determine when the asset can operate at full output and start generating its expected return.

The commercial consequences can be significant. A delay to operation can mean deferred revenue alongside extended financing, project management, insurance and other holding costs. Depending on the project, it can also affect offtake arrangements and the expected investment return. For owners and investors, the milestone that matters is when the asset can energise and start earning, rather than when construction finishes.

Capacity needs to be considered across the whole delivery system

The constraints seen most consistently are grid and connection capacity, and the specialist capability needed to design, deliver and commission projects. The workforce issue is more specific than a general shortage of construction workers. Energy is competing with transmission, data centres, defence, housing and other infrastructure programs for overlapping skills, with pressure most evident in high-voltage electrical, protection and control, grid compliance and commissioning. These skills take time and experience to develop and cannot be scaled quickly simply by adding people.

Sequencing compounds the problem. A project program can be perfectly logical in isolation and still become difficult to deliver once the network, equipment and specialist resources it depends on are considered. Several projects may each make reasonable assumptions about contractor availability, commissioning resources or network interfaces, yet collectively require more capacity than the market can provide in the same delivery window. For owners with multiple projects, that makes portfolio-level sequencing increasingly important.

Earlier procurement is not automatically better

Long-lead electrical equipment adds further complexity, because protecting an energisation date may require major equipment decisions before every technical and connection requirement is settled. Waiting provides greater design certainty but can expose the program to manufacturing lead times. Committing early may secure capacity, but it increases the risk of later specification changes, variations or stranded expenditure. Project teams need to understand which decisions genuinely control the commercial-operation date, when they must be made and what uncertainty remains at that point.

Contracting raises a similar issue. Connection, interface and program risks can be transferred into an EPC or another delivery contract, but risk allocation does not remove delivery risk. Someone will still price it, qualify it or ultimately carry it. Better outcomes come from reducing uncertainty wherever practical, then allocating the remaining risk to the parties best able to manage it.

Plan backwards from commercial operation

For owners and investors, this points to a relatively simple change in approach. Instead of developing a construction program and fitting connection and commissioning around it, start with the required commercial-operation date and work backwards. That means bringing network readiness, connection maturity, equipment decisions, testing, commissioning and specialist resourcing into feasibility much earlier. Owners managing multiple projects should also test their portfolio against market capacity, rather than assuming every project can independently access the contractors, specialists, equipment and network windows it needs.

There will always be uncertainty. Different technologies, locations and network conditions create different delivery challenges. The aim is to understand those uncertainties early enough for the investment case, cost plan, procurement strategy and program to reflect how the project can realistically be delivered.

Australia has shown it can bring significant volumes of renewable generation and storage into operation. The test now is whether we can sustain and scale that delivery, because the value of the pipeline ultimately depends on how effectively it is converted into operating capacity.

Author: Jack Shelley, State Director, WT

item.title: Australia’s wasted solar: much of the fix is already installed
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Curtailment across the National Electricity Market continues to reach new highs, and whilst additional transmission capacity is certainly needed, it remains some years off. Interestingly, a significant proportion of the equipment that could help absorb this surplus energy has already been installed, although at present it is not yet operating in a coordinated manner.
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday 11 October 2026, a little after midday, Victoria was curtailing 5,709 MW of renewable generation. That’s a record for the state. It came 15 minutes after rooftop solar across the National Electricity Market (NEM) set a record of its own.

The NEM curtailed 2.93 TWh of wind and solar in the first half of this year, which is 37% more than the same period last year and about 7% of everything wind and solar produced. The Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) September quarter report then showed network curtailment averaging 281 MW, roughly double what it was a year earlier, with solar farms in New South Wales (NSW) taking the biggest hit.

The typical response to this challenge is to call for more transmission infrastructure, and indeed, that is required. However, new transmission lines take considerable time to deliver, and they do little to address the other form of curtailment; where prices turn negative during the middle of the day and generators choose to switch off rather than pay to export. What is needed in these instances is a means to absorb this excess energy during peak solar generation, and, in fact, much of the necessary equipment has already been procured and installed.

The kit is there. It isn’t working together yet

So what is already available? According to AEMO, rooftop solar now stands at about 27 GW, distributed across 3.9 million installations, and more than 600,000 home batteries have been installed under the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. Grid-scale batteries are also playing an increasingly active role. In the September quarter, they shifted more than three times the energy they did a year earlier, and at present, they are absorbing approximately 13 GWh of daytime power each day.

There has been some progress, albeit limited. According to figures from Rystad Energy, utility-scale solar curtailment fell to 22% of available generation in September, down from 26% the previous September, as additional battery capacity was brought online. This is certainly a step in the right direction, although it is worth noting that 22% still represents a significant proportion of potential generation that is not being utilised.

One thing that is often missed is the difference between just owning the assets (batteries, inverters, controllable hot water) and actually having those assets be able to respond when the grid needs them.

These devices are supplied by a wide range of manufacturers, each utilising different software platforms and communication protocols. While it is relatively straightforward to control a single device at the appropriate moment, orchestrating the coordinated operation of hundreds of thousands of such devices, alongside large-scale batteries and local solar farms, as grid conditions fluctuate throughout the day, presents a far more complex challenge. In practice, this is primarily a matter of software and systems integration.

To illustrate the complexity involved, one of the more common challenges encountered in managing large fleets of devices is that a firmware update can subtly alter the meaning of a particular data register. The battery itself may be functioning correctly, as may the inverter, but the coordinating system may now be interpreting the data incorrectly. When this issue is multiplied across an entire fleet, it becomes clear why there is often a significant gap between installed capacity and actual usable flexibility.

Decide centrally, execute locally

This raises the question of where coordination should reside. A useful rule of thumb is to make decisions centrally but execute them locally. Activities such as forecasting, trading, and portfolio optimisation are best managed in the cloud, where a comprehensive view of the market is available. However, the actual control should be implemented at the site, in close proximity to the asset itself.

There are several reasons for this approach. Firstly, speed is critical, as certain grid services require a response within approximately one second, and relying on a round trip to a remote data centre is not feasible in such cases. Secondly, resilience is important. If a site loses its external connection, it should continue to operate within its grid constraints and manage the battery appropriately, rather than waiting for further instructions. Thirdly, from a data perspective, it is considerably more efficient to process and normalise telemetry locally, rather than transmitting all raw data to the cloud for subsequent processing.

This approach is already established practice at the larger end of the market. For example, at IOTech, our edge software is integrated into the battery systems of one of the world’s largest grid-scale storage providers, which has more than 20 GW under management worldwide using our solution. In these systems, the control path is entirely local and does not rely on any off-site infrastructure. The edge nodes communicate with each device using its native protocol and translate the responses into a unified data model, which means that integrating a new inverter or battery does not require starting the integration process from the beginning.

This same approach needs to be extended to commercial sites and residential properties, as this is where a significant proportion of new flexibility is being deployed. This, in turn, prompts several practical considerations for those procuring or specifying such equipment. For example, how does the device behave if it loses connectivity partway through an instruction? Is it possible to control the device locally via an open interface, or is it restricted to the manufacturer’s cloud platform? Will it remain compatible with the rest of the fleet following future updates?

It is important to emphasise that none of this is a substitute for new transmission infrastructure. Australia will still require additional lines, as well as further generation and storage capacity. However, in the coming springs and summers, the grid is likely to experience increasing volumes of midday solar generation that cannot be fully utilised, and the new transmission lines will not yet be operational. The most immediate improvements are likely to come from enabling the existing installed equipment to operate in a more coordinated manner, much of which has already been paid for.

Author: Andy Foster, Chief Product Officer, IOTech Systems

item.title: Rainfall alone cannot eliminate bird-dropping soiling on solar panels, study finds
item.dc:creator: Emiliano Bellini
item.description: An international research team has found that bird-dropping soiling can cause annual PV performance losses of around 6%. The researchers also found that conventional soiling models underestimate these losses, highlighting the need for improved modeling approaches and cleaning strategies.
item.content:encoded:
n international research team has conducted a year-long experimental study to assess the impact of bird droppings on PV system performance and has found that soiling losses stabilized after a prolonged accumulation period, remaining at consistent levels despite repeated rainfall events.

“Our paper highlights this limitation, but we cannot yet provide a solution,” corresponding author Leonardo Micheli told pv magazine. “Factors such as bird activity and proximity to nesting areas are likely to influence soiling accumulation under these conditions, but further research is needed to identify the quantitative variables that could be used to reliably model this type of soiling.”

“Our study demonstrates that a monitoring approach based on clean irradiance measurements can successfully estimate soiling losses caused by bird droppings, without the need to maintain a clean reference module,” Micheli added. “However, we also show that its accuracy depends on calibration. Furthermore, accuracy could also be influenced by operating conditions, and further validation across different sites is needed to confirm its general applicability.”

“We show that rainfall does not necessarily restore modules to clean conditions: significant soiling losses can persist even after repeated natural cleaning events,” he said. “The existence of this phenomenon has already been discussed in the literature, and our study confirms its relevance in environments affected by bird droppings, as this can be particularly difficult to remove. This challenges the common modelling assumption that rainfall effectively removes accumulated soiling and should be considered when optimizing cleaning schedules and costs. A rainy period should not be taken as evidence that PV modules are free from soiling.”

The experimental setup consisted of two monocrystalline JA Solar JAM54S30-410/MR silicon modules installed at ground level at the University of Split, Croatia. One module served as a clean reference, while the other was left to accumulate natural soiling. Both were mounted on an open rack with identical tilt, azimuth, and height to ensure comparable environmental and irradiance conditions.

The researchers conducted weekly measurements from July 2024 to July 2025. During each session, they recorded four current-voltage (I-V) curves per module using an EKO Instruments MP-11 tracer, while also measuring irradiance and module temperature. Measurements were taken near solar noon under clear skies and stable irradiance conditions, in accordance with IEC 61724-1.

The researchers calculated the soiling ratio by comparing the short-circuit currents of the soiled and clean modules. They also tested an alternative approach that estimates clean-module output using irradiance and temperature data. In addition, they evaluated three established soiling models based on particulate matter concentrations and rainfall. Two models assumed complete cleaning when daily rainfall exceeded 1 mm, while the third accounted for partial cleaning.

The researchers recorded an average soiling ratio of 0.941 over the monitoring period, corresponding to performance losses of approximately 6%, or an estimated 72.1 kWh/kWp annually. The ratio fell below 0.90 in November 2024 following a prolonged dry period, with bird droppings identified as the main source of contamination. Subsequent rainfall events only partially restored module performance, with the soiling ratio stabilizing at around 0.94 to 0.96.

A second accumulation period in April and May 2025 reduced the ratio to approximately 0.90, resulting in estimated daily energy losses of 0.41 kWh/kW and 0.47 kWh/kW, respectively.

The researchers found that only manual cleaning fully restored module performance. Their analysis also showed that the three conventional soiling models systematically underestimated losses because they relied primarily on particulate matter concentrations and assumptions about rainfall-induced cleaning.

They concluded that existing models cannot adequately capture the accumulation and removal of bird droppings, particularly in urban environments. They also recommended incorporating additional soiling measurements, more detailed rainfall characteristics, and saturation effects into future models.

“Overall, the results highlight that the applicability of current soiling modelling approaches is strongly dependent on the deposition mechanisms. Clearly, in environments where soiling is not dominated by gradual particulate accumulation, estimates based on current models may be unreliable,” the researchers stated.

Their findings are presented in “Mind the birds: Assessing the uncertainty in modelling of urban photovoltaic soiling,” published in Solar Energy. The research team included scientists from the University of Split in Croatia and Sapienza University of Rome in Italy.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: BloombergNEF forecasts 215 GW of solar in Australia by 2050
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australia’s solar capacity is forecast to reach up to 215 GW by 2050, up from 43 GW in 2025, as falling costs continue to strengthen the economics of utility-scale renewables.
item.content:encoded:
New modelling from Bloomberg New Energy Finance (BNEF) shows solar emerging as the largest component of Australia’s power fleet by mid-century, with capacity growing from 43 GW in 2025 to 137 GW under a business-as-usual scenario or 215 GW under a more accelerated transition.

In the latest edition of its New Energy Outlook Australia report, BNEF has modelled a net zero scenario (NZS), that achieves fully decarbonised power, transport, industry and buildings by 2050, and a base-case economy transition scenario (ETS), that lays out how commercially available technologies could be deployed with no further policy support beyond existing measures.

The modelling shows Australia’s solar capacity growing from 43 GW in 2025 to 137 GW by mid-century under the ETS. Under the NZS, capacity reaches 215 GW, more than five times the 2025 level.

BNEF said under both models, solar emerges as the largest component of Australia’s power fleet by 2050, its dominance in the power mix reflecting the country’s “high-quality solar resource and the continued cost advantage of both utility-scale and rooftop solar.”

Onshore wind capacity reaches 61 GW by 2050 under the ETS, up from 15 GW in 2025, while it reaches 107 GW by mid-century under the NZS.

Stationary battery storage capacity is forecast to expand from 5 GW in 2025 to 45 GW under the ETS and 50 GW under the NZS by 2050. BNEF said the larger fleet under the NZS reflects the need for greater flexibility in a system with higher electricity demand and a larger share of variable renewable generation.

Despite the continued expansion of Australia’s installed wind and solar capacity, BNEF warns the market will struggle to reach the federal government’s renewable energy target of 82% share of generation by 2030.

The modelling shows Australia is likely to deliver just 64% renewables by the end of the decade under the NZS, with renewables only reaching 61% by 2030 in the ETS. Under the NZS, Australia does not reach the 82% renewables target until 2035. The ETS remains further behind, with renewables reaching 78% generation by 2035.

BNEF Australia Senior Associate and report author Sahaj Sood said persistent renewable development constraints, including slow grid expansion, social-license concerns and permitting challenges, and growing power demand may have put 2030 target out of reach.

“Net zero fundamentally changes the scale of Australia’s power system,” he said. “Electricity demand more than doubles by 2050, requiring a much faster buildout of wind, solar, storage and network capacity.”

“The technologies are increasingly cost-competitive but building them at the pace and scale required will depend on removing the infrastructure, permitting and grid bottlenecks that continue to slow deployment.”

The report shows Australia’s power demand rises substantially through to 2050 under both scenarios, but more sharply under the NZS as electrification extends further across the economy. Demand reaches 339 TWh by 2050 under the ETS, up 50% from 2025, compared with 506 TWh under the NZS – 49% above the ETS and 123% higher than 2025 levels.

Electric vehicles are a major source of new power demand in both scenarios. EV demand reaches 52 TWh by 2050 under the ETS, equivalent to 15% of total power demand, and 69 TWh under the NZS, or 14%. Data centres also become a more material source of load, accounting for 38 TWh of demand by mid-century in both scenarios.

BNEF said the uptake of renewable will continue to is driven by falling costs. Benchmark levelised costs of electricity (LCOEs) are about $44 per MWh for single axis tracking solar and $77/MWh for onshore wind in 2025. Both are already below the cost of building new coal- or gas-fired generation capacity.

In BNEF’s modelling, renewable costs decline through 2050. Solar remains the cheapest new-build technology, with its LCOE falling 63% to about $16/MWh, while onshore wind declines 34% to about $51/MWh.

item.title: Researchers test new tech to help bring solar and storage to apartments
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: An AI-powered energy system is being installed at an apartment complex in Sydney’s south as part of a $1.2 million project designed to expand access to rooftop solar and battery storage for Australians living in apartments.
item.content:encoded:
A modular power portal system (MPPS) that brings together rooftop solar generation, battery storage and intelligent energy management is being installed at an apartment complex in southern Sydney to test how rooftop solar and shared battery storage can supply electricity across multiple tenancies.

The system, being installed at a residential building in the southern Sydney suburb of Wolli Creek, combines an AI-powered energy system developed by researchers at the University of New South Wales (UNSW) Canberra with a MPPS developed by Sydney-headquartered clean tech companies JT Solar Technology and Voltval.

The building’s new rooftop array will feature 350 solar panels, providing about 154 kW of generation capacity. The panels will be paired with a 200 kWh battery energy storage system and a separate 200 kWh community battery, giving the site a planned combined storage capacity of 400 kWh.

Connections to participating apartments will follow the infrastructure installation, with UNSW’s AI-based energy management system to then be added to optimise how energy is managed and shared across the building.

The install is part of a $1.2 million (USD 800,000) research partnership between UNSW, JT Solar Technology, and Voltval. Supported through the Australian government’s Trailblazer for Recycling and Clean Energy (TRaCE) program, the partnership is designed to give apartment residents the same access to rooftop solar and battery storage that many households in standalone homes already enjoy.

TRaCE said the Wolli Creek install is the first in a multi-site pilot combining commercial and residential sites across Sydney, and a key step in moving the MPPS from development into commercial use.

“Wolli Creek is a starting point,” it said. “Performance data from the site will guide deployment at further pilot sites and help extend MPPS beyond apartments to a range of built environments.”

While Australia leads the world in rooftop solar uptake, the benefits have largely bypassed the more than 2.5 million Australians who live in apartments. In New South Wales – where one in five homes is an apartment – UNSW data shows just 3.5% of apartment dwellers have access to rooftop solar.

Jason Xiao, Director of JT Solar Technology, said it is hoped the combined technologies will be capable of forecasting energy generation and demand, coordinating distributed energy resources, and balance electricity flows between apartments in real time.

“We believe we are definitely making our development work smarter and will benefit everyone,” he said. “The limitations of renewable energy in apartments will be minimised.”

Voltval Director Steve Doyle said the partners are already thinking about the next frontier for shared energy systems.

“Another area we are exploring is bidirectional EV charging, which could bring greater flexibility and convenience to multi-tenant buildings,” he said.

“We see significant potential in integrating this technology into shared energy systems, creating more opportunities for residents and building owners to benefit from smarter energy management.”

The goal is to give apartment residents the same access to rooftop solar that many households in standalone homes already enjoy.

item.title: Why New Zealand households are taking solar seriously in 2026
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: New Zealand’s residential solar market is evolving with 2026 delivering a milestone year after energy security became a much more personal conversation. Rising power bills were already getting people’s attention. Then the war in Iran gave them something else to think about.
item.content:encoded:
The New Zealand residential solar market operates quite differently to its Australian counterpart. Kiwi homeowners get no upfront solar subsidy, no battery rebate, and no net metering. Energy retailers pay for exports, but the economics are built around using your own solar generation.

The NZ solar industry had to make the numbers stack up without much help from the government. That’s made growth frustratingly slow at times, but steadier, without the booms and busts that come with incentives being switched on and off.

The biggest helping hand has come from the big banks, with mortgage top-ups for solar and batteries at 1% for three years or 0% for five years. They’ve been a key growth driver for years. Long may they last, but banks can pull them at any time.

Even so, the market is on a growth curve.

2026 at a glance (January to mid-November)

  • 13,282 new residential solar installations, already more than all of 2025.
  • 87,734 homes with solar (4.3% of homes), totalling 523 MW.
  • 8.7 kW – the average new residential system size, up from 3.3 kW a decade ago.
  • $2.04 per watt average price for solar, the same as 2025.
  • About half of new home systems include a battery: 48% in our survey, around 53% in Electricity Authority data.
  • $33,000 average for a solar and battery package.

Sources: Electricity Authority data to October 2026 and the My Solar Quotes 2026 homeowner survey. Prices are NZD, including GST; the price-per-watt figure excludes batteries.

The fuel shock brought buyers forward

The war in Iran landed in a country already thinking harder about resilience after several years of severe weather events. Then fuel prices jumped, and energy security suddenly had a very visible price tag.

Some households responded by buying an EV. Once your transport runs off your power bill, solar is a natural next step. Making fuel on your own roof has an obvious appeal to the Kiwi instinct for looking after yourself.

At My Solar Quotes, we saw our biggest ever surge in enquiries. Installers told me the same, with some booked six to eight months ahead.

That urgency eased as expensive fuel became part of the household budget. The vulnerabilities hadn’t gone away; people just got used to them.

I see that surge as households bringing forward decisions they were already considering. The fuel shock supplied the urgency. Electricity prices supplied the ongoing reason.

The real driver: climbing power bills

The average annual household electricity bill is now about NZD 2,617 (2,151). Average electricity costs have risen 46% in a decade, reaching 42.1 cents per kWh.

Network investment is adding to the squeeze as lines companies renew ageing infrastructure and expand capacity for electrification. Meanwhile, the average fixed charge of NZD 2.70 a day costs households nearly NZD 990 a year before they use a single unit of electricity. Households can improve their energy efficiency and still find themselves paying more.

Solar lets Kiwis buy less power from the grid and earn a bit of cheddar by selling their surplus back.

Geopolitics triggered a rush of buyers earlier this year, but rising power prices remain the market’s most consistent driver. With the cost of living front of mind for voters, they also gave politicians an obvious place to start making promises.

Then the politicians brought out the carrots

Ahead of the 7 November election, solar became a prominent political offering. Promises ranged from cheaper, more accessible finance to Labour’s subsidy offer of up to NZD 3,000 for low- and middle-income households.

After years of governments leaving residential solar to its own devices, it was quite something to see everyone arrive with a carrot.

For some households, though, the response was to wait. Enquiries have been noticeably quieter for the past few months as buyers wait to see which promises become policy. Elections make buyers cautious anyway; the prospect of financial help gives them another reason to sit tight.

For installers carrying months of booked work, that pause has provided a useful breather.

I’m skeptical that a government-backed loan will move the needle much for households already eligible for cheap bank finance. The bigger opportunity is reaching those who currently miss out. Longer repayment terms could help too, but the fine print will determine how far these schemes actually widen access. Who qualifies, and on what terms, is what I’ll be watching.

Bigger systems, same price

Solar prices held steady during 2025 at NZD 2 per watt, unchanged from 2025. That’s despite higher panel costs after China scrapped its export tax rebate in April, freight rates more than doubling and a weaker Kiwi dollar.

But that steady average hides a small price rise. Like-for-like prices crept up a few percent across most system sizes. Kiwis are simply installing bigger systems, which cost less per watt and kept the overall average flat.

That shift is a long-running trend. The average new home system has more than doubled in a decade, from around 3.3 kW to close to 9 kW. The last two years have been the fastest yet, with the average climbing more than a kW a year, from 6.4 kW in 2024 to 7.6 kW in 2025 and 8.7 kW this year. Cheap panels, batteries and low-interest bank loans all made it easy to fill the roof.

Half of buyers now add a battery – with no rebate

The most interesting change is batteries. Australia needed a federal rebate to get home batteries moving. New Zealand has nothing, yet about half of new home solar systems now include one, up from about 29% in 2024.

I’ve had people tell me, “Solar doesn’t really work without a battery.” Yeah, nah. It absolutely does. But somewhere along the way, Kiwis seem to have convinced themselves the two have to come as a package.

Median payback is seven years for solar only and nine years with a battery.

Battery buyers tell us the main reason is to use more of their own solar, followed by backup during blackouts.

Tesla Powerwall 3 and Sigenergy made up more than 70% of the batteries in our survey, and battery buyers also go bigger on solar, averaging 10.1 kW compared with 8.1 kW for solar-only homes.

Our batteries are still small by Australian standards, though. The average Kiwi battery in our survey was 11.5 kWh, and the most common size was 13.5 kWh, roughly half the Australian average of about 22 kWh. Without a rebate, upfront cost is what stops many from going bigger.

Solar power system installed in Hawke’s Bay by Ecoefficient

Where to from here?

New Zealand is past the early adopter stage – a long haul, but we got there. Solar is becoming normal, and we may be at the start of an exponential curve. A typical solar and battery system costs NZD 30,000 to NZD 35,000, but most buyers can justify it to bring down their power bills.

There is plenty of room to grow. Roughly one in 25 Kiwi homes has solar, compared with more than 30% of Australian households.

The risks are the ones you’d expect: cheap bank finance could disappear, and a sudden surge in demand could stretch installers and invite poor workmanship. Government incentives could be a positive or equally a hindrance – yet to be seen.

But if this year has shown anything, it’s that New Zealanders don’t need a rebate to go solar. They need high power bills, affordable finance and confidence that the numbers stack up. Right now, they have all three.

Author: Kristy Hoare, founder, Mysolarquotes.co.nz

item.title: Gaotu unveils foldable off-grid solar EV charger
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Gaotu Innovation, a manufacturer of portable and distributed PV hardware, has introduced a car-mounted EV charging solution into the Australian market that pairs a 1,600 W expandable solar array with a 2.5 kWh battery pack.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese manufacturer Gaotu Innovation has unveiled an off-grid electric vehicle (EV) charging system designed to address the “unique challenges” associated with Australia’s rural and outback regions.

Gaotu said the all-in-one GT‑EV16‑PB‑FD charger integrates a foldable PV array that delivers a maximum solar input power of 1,600 W with a 2.5 kWh lithium‑iron‑phosphate battery pack.

The manufacturer said the system is capable of providing up to 80 kilometres of daily driving range, completely independent of the grid, and is “a game-changer for EV owners” in Australia.

“Many Australian EV owners face charging gaps when travelling in remote areas or going camping,” the company said. “Our roof‑mount solar EV charger allows drivers to harvest energy directly from sunlight, independent of public charging stations.”

The GT‑EV16‑PB‑FD system is equipped with dual independent MPPT trackers that Gaotu said support a maximum PV input of 800 W ×2, with MPPT efficiency up to 99.9 % while the solar panels deliver a cell‑level conversion efficiency of 25%.

The solar is paired with a built‑in 2.5 kWh battery pack that acts as an essential buffer, absorbing incoming energy spikes and delivering regulated AC power straight into the vehicle inlet. Smart APP control via Bluetooth and Wi‑Fi enables remote charging management.

Designed for vehicle‑roof installation, Gaotu said the foldable solar array is housed in an IP68 -rated enclosure while the aerodynamic design to withstand wind speeds up to 160 kph. The unfolded dimension of the solar array is 3,350 cm × 2,310 cm.

The system’s operating temperature ranges from ‑20 °C to +55 °C, and the first‑year power degradation is about 1%, followed by maximum 0.4% annual degradation in subsequent years. The product comes with a five‑year workmanship warranty and a two‑year power‑performance warranty.

In addition to EV charging, Gaotu said the unit can also act as an off‑grid UPS power supply.

“When mains power drops, seamless switch‑over within 10 ms guarantees continuous power output,” the company said.

Besides complete units for local distributors, Gaotu said it also offers full OEM and ODM customisation for Australian partners.

item.title: How did the COP31 climate agreement fall apart – and what happens now?
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, came to an end – but not as we might have hoped.
item.content:encoded:
Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.

Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

No mention of the ‘F’ word

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable.

Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels,” marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations.

The Dubai text was hailed as “the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era.” But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Turkey.

In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text.

Australia and Turkey proposed a compromise – no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy.”

This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text.

Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda.

The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Turkey and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps.

Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Turkey in his speech at the summit opening. While Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects.

Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship “35 by 35” electrification pledge. The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23% at present to 35% by 2035.

Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on, including the European Union and China.

The “COP of action” fails to deliver

This year’s climate summit was billed as an “implementation COP”, focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change.

Overseen by Australia in its role as “president of negotiations,” the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate.

It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so.

African countries, in particular, stressed that an “implementation COP” was meaningless if rich nations failed to provide the actual resources needed to act.

Despite the general gloom, these talks did achieve progress in a few areas. Nations moved forwards on supporting a just transition (shifting to clean energy fairly) via a “phased approach”, as well as improving alignment in climate adaptation, which will help the poorest nations to implement their adaptation plans.

But broader efforts to find a way forward on the Paris Agreement’s Global Goal on Adaptation were left unresolved.

Decisions stalled in many negotiating rooms in the face of hard “red lines” declared by different blocs of countries.

Countries failed to reach any agreement on the vital question of cutting emissions, after Saudia Arabia and Russia blocked a proposed decision. Both are among the world’s top fossil fuel exporting nations.

This failure has left the world without any dedicated negotiating process on cutting emissions under the Paris Agreement. It’s possible nations could agree to renew a work program on climate mitigation at next year’s COP32 talks in Ethiopia.

What about money for adaptation?

Who pays for the costs of climate change has long been a contentious point. Developing countries face the brunt of damage from climate change, but have emitted far less – and have much less money to spend on adaptation.

Ahead of COP31, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said talks on new climate finance commitments were “dead in the water.” He urged delegates to focus on implementing existing pledges rather than try for fresh funding.

The summit failed to meet even these low expectations. No concrete progress was achieved on the goal of tripling funds for climate adaptation pledged last year at COP30 in Brazil.

Ahead of the summit, the Australian government flagged the need to boost global contributions to the official Pacific climate fund.

This, too, didn’t eventuate. Rich nations – including Australia – merely re-announced their existing pledges, leaving the Pacific fund A$450 million short of its 2026 target of $749 million.

Ironically, the most notable pledge came from the Solomon Islands, a small Pacific nation. Prime Minister Matthew Wale pledged $600,000 to the global Green Climate Fund. “The Pacific did not create this crisis,” he declared. “But we will not stand by and wait for others to act”.

A few new commitments arrived by the end of the two week summit from nations such as Canada and Norway.

Defending the science

Unusually, climate science was front and centre at COP31.

This year, a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries has been obstructing the publication of key scientific reports from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

This year marks the first UN summit since it was officially confirmed the world will overshoot the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal by 2030.

With the collapse of support for the cover text, statements supporting release of the latest climate science didn’t get approval. All that remained were technical conclusions which “expressed utmost concern” that climate impacts will continue to increase with every increment of global warming.

Australia on the global stage

COP31 gave Australia a unique global role. After being outmanoeuvred in their bid to host the summit, Australia secured a role in overseeing negotiations.

Australian Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and his team had the unenviable task of seeking consensus between 195 countries and the European Union.

After the cover text was rejected, Bowen declared Australia had left “nothing on the field” but had faced “unbridgeable red lines.”

Hours beforehand, Fijian Climate Minister Lynda Tabuya acknowledged Bowen’s efforts, noting the failure was “not yours to carry […] it is the responsibility of all parties.”

Are COP summits still worthwhile?

This year’s climate summit took the unenviable record of the longest ever. With consensus seemingly impossible, some civil society representatives dubbed it “the worst COP ever.”

Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blamed “powerful fossil fuel interests,” including fossil fuel exporters and corporate lobbyists.

Some nations are now calling for urgent reform to negotiations long paralysed by vetoes and disconnected from science.

Unfortunately, any change to official voting processes would itself require a consensus decision.

Consensus is hard to achieve, but powerful. The power of the Paris Agreement draws on the fact it represents the view of nearly every country – big or small, rich or poor.

COP31 President Murat Kurum began the summit expressing hopes this year’s talks would leave a legacy of “working together.”

That was a false hope. A more realistic hope is that the collapse of consensus may be the shock the world needs to change course.

As former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has said, we should not see the refusal of more than 130 countries to sign an inadequate deal as a failure. Rather, it might be “a sign of courage.”

Authors: Jacqueline Peel, Professor of Law, The University of Melbourne; Kathryn Bowen, Director, Melbourne Climate Futures and Professor – Environment, Climate and Global Health at Melbourne Climate Futures and Melbourne School of Population and Global Health, The University of Melbourne
